card.title: Merge a branch back
card.blurb: One command brings a branch home - and it does two different things. Run `git merge` when `main` stayed put, then again when it did not.
hero.eyebrow: Git · Part three · Bringing work back
hero.title: Merge a branch back
intro.0: Your branch works, and now it has to become part of `main`. That is the step people hesitate over - it feels like where things get broken. It is one command, and it behaves in two different ways. Which way you get depends on nothing you type: only on whether `main` moved while you were away. Here you run it both ways and watch the graph answer for you.
task.1.title: Bring it back when `main` stayed put
task.1.context:
You made `fix`, committed `add dog` there, and switched back. `main` has not moved since the split, so `fix` is simply ahead of it.

`git merge fix` brings that branch's commits into the one you are on. Here there is nothing to combine, so git takes the cheap route.
task.1.goal.1: Both names should end up on the same commit, `add dog`.
task.1.goal.2: Nothing new is saved - that is a fast-forward.
task.2.title: Bring it back when both sides moved
task.2.context:
Same branch, one difference: after switching back you also committed `feed the cat` on `main`. Each side now holds a commit the other has never seen.

Sliding a name forward would leave one of them off the line, so `git merge fix` has to do the other thing.
task.2.goal.1: A commit appears that neither branch had before.
task.2.goal.2: It has two parents - one line running back to each side.
task.3.title: Merge a branch back - recap
task.3.context: One command, two shapes - decided by where the names were sitting.
task.3.summaryIntro: Merging is not one fixed move. Git looks at whether the branch you are standing on has added anything since the split, and then picks the smallest thing that works.
task.3.summaryItems.0.title: Merge -
task.3.summaryItems.0.text: bringing another branch's commits into the one you are on, so two lines become one.
task.3.summaryItems.1.title: Fast-forward -
task.3.summaryItems.1.text: what you get when your branch added nothing; git slides its name forward and saves no commit.
task.3.summaryItems.2.title: Merge commit -
task.3.summaryItems.2.text: what you get when both sides moved; it is the one commit with two parents.
task.3.summaryItems.3.title: `git merge fix` -
task.3.summaryItems.3.text: the same line either way, so read the graph to see which one you got.
task.3.summaryClose: Next: what happens when both sides changed the same file, and git stops to ask you.
